selection.text: A dose-response curve plots the magnitude and direction of a measurable effect (e.g., drug efficacy or toxicity) against the administered dose of the stimulus on the x‑axis, showing how the response changes with increasing exposure. The curve typically rises, plateaus, or falls depending on the biological system’s response pattern to the dose. A peak at an intermediate dose can occur because many physiological responses have an activation threshold (low doses produce little or no effect), become saturated or reach functional limits at moderate doses (e.g., all receptors bound), and at higher doses adverse, inhibitory, or damaging effects may emerge, causing the response to decline after the peak.
